 Opening Statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates)
 Michele Bullock 
 Governor 
 Senate Economics Legislation Committee (Supplementary Budget Estimates) 
 28 October 2026 
 – Videoconference 
 Live now 
 Good morning, Chair and members of the Committee.
 My colleagues and I are here today to answer your questions.
 As you know, our purpose is to promote the economic prosperity and welfare of the Australian people, now
 and into the future. One way we do this is by setting monetary policy to achieve low and stable inflation
 and full employment, and by supporting the stability of the financial system. But we also promote the
 prosperity and welfare of Australians across the full range of our responsibilities, which include
 supporting a reliable, efficient and competitive payments system, delivering efficient and effective
 banking services to Australian government agencies, and providing secure and reliable banknotes to
 Australians.
 Since the Committee’s previous hearing with the RBA in June, the Monetary Policy Board has increased
 the cash rate target by 25 basis points. It did this with the goal of returning inflation to target.
 This has taken the cumulative increase in the cash rate target this year to 100 basis points. I will
 start with some background to these decisions and the outlook for the Australian economy. I’ll then
 provide an update on the payments system and cash distribution.
 Recent monetary policy decisions and the economic outlook
 As you know, the Monetary Policy Board sets monetary policy such that inflation is expected to return to
 the midpoint of the 2–3 per cent target range. There is some
 flexibility around the timeframe over which we meet our inflation objective, to balance this with meeting
 our full employment objective. But it is important for the economy that inflation does not diverge from
 target for too long, since that risks it becoming embedded in inflation expectations, which feeds through
 to price and wage-setting decisions.
 Inflation fell significantly from its peak of 7.9 per cent at the end of 2022 to be within the
 2–3 per cent target range for a period in 2024 and 2025. This followed
 a significant tightening of monetary policy over 2022 and 2023. But inflation picked up over the second
 half of 2025 and has remained above target since then. Recently, inflation has been around 3½ to
 4 per cent in year-ended terms. The increase in inflation reflects both persistent capacity
 pressures in the Australian economy and global cost pressures associated with the conflict in the Middle
 East. Because of both these factors, inflation is likely to remain elevated for some time.
 Our most recent published forecasts – in the August Statement on Monetary Policy 
 – suggested that inflation would not return to around the midpoint of the target range until late
 2027. At the time of the August Board meeting, we assessed that the risks to that outlook were skewed to
 the upside.
 Developments since then suggest that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing as expected,
 some of the international and domestic upside risks to inflation have materialised or are materialising.
 Inflation will therefore likely be higher than was our base case in August.
 The conflict in the Middle East has re-escalated and global energy prices are now much higher than had
 been assumed in the August forecasts. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add
 materially to inflation, both directly and indirectly as businesses facing increasing pressures from
 higher transport and related costs attempt to pass them on. At the same time, short-term inflation
 expectations are elevated.
 Other global cost pressures have increased. In addition to the energy price shock, the AI boom and extreme
 weather events are contributing to upward pressure on a range of agricultural and technology-related
 prices. The global AI boom is also driving stronger growth in economies that are key parts of the AI
 supply chain. In turn, that is driving higher global prices for some AI-related technologies that are
 supply constrained.
 Importantly though, it is not just these global pressures that are driving inflation in Australia. While
 they are certainly compounding the inflation problem, we still see inflation arising from domestic
 capacity pressures. Despite the unemployment rate recently rising a little more than we had expected, the
 labour market seems a little tighter than we had previously judged. The evidence for this is elevated
 underlying inflationary pressures. That is, when we exclude some of the large volatile price movements
 such as fuel we see inflationary pressure in areas that reflect domestic demand for goods and services.
 And continued weak productivity growth means that the economy cannot grow strongly without putting
 pressure on inflation. This is a fundamental challenge for the Australian economy and for everyone’s
 real spending power over the next few years.
 Against this backdrop, and despite growth in domestic demand slowing, a further period of subdued growth
 of aggregate demand is needed to reduce capacity pressures and bring inflation down sustainably.
 We are not alone in being concerned about inflation – central banks in many other advanced economies
 are responding by increasing their policy rates or signalling they will do so if needed.
 Because monetary policy works with a lag, the full effects of recent rate increases are yet to be felt on
 domestic activity. The impact of the conflict in the Middle East on economic activity has been relatively
 modest so far. Household spending growth has been moderating only gradually. And business investment
 growth has picked up strongly, driven mostly by spending on data centres and renewable energy projects.
 The share of the population with a job remains high. This is a welcome outcome for those individuals,
 their families and the wider Australian economy.
 Conditions in the housing market have softened, reflecting the usual transmission of monetary policy, but
 also tax policy changes and the broader economic environment. Housing prices have fallen in most capital
 cities and new housing loans have declined. This follows a long period of strong growth, however,
 underpinned by a structural undersupply of housing. And housing prices are around 50 per cent
 higher than they were in early 2020. Financial stability risks from household borrowing remain contained:
 while many are facing budget pressures, only a small share of borrowers are in negative equity or facing
 severe repayment difficulty. I recognise how challenging it is for those experiencing these issues.
 I want to emphasise that, while we expect housing prices to be affected when interest rates rise, monetary
 policy does not target housing prices. Rather, what matters is how changes in housing prices affect
 economic activity, the labour market and, ultimately, inflation.
 The Monetary Policy Board will meet next week. We’ll discuss our assessment of the flow of data and
 how the risks are unfolding. A key question is whether the tightening in monetary policy to date will be
 sufficient to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time. We are committed to our mandate to
 deliver price stability and full employment.
 I recognise that higher interest rates can be difficult, particularly for households with mortgages who
 are also facing cost-of-living pressures. But we can’t allow high inflation to persist. High
 inflation hurts everyone. It means higher grocery costs, higher rent, and higher electricity bills. It
 makes everyone’s pay packets and savings worth less – and it particularly hurts people with
 lower incomes and little savings.
 Monetary policy affects all parts of the economy, not just households with mortgages – it influences
 the spending, saving and borrowing decisions of all households and businesses. I am happy to expand on
 this in the Q&A.
 Payments system
 Another key responsibility for the RBA is the regulation and oversight of the payments system.
 We have completed our review of surcharging and merchant card payment costs. Following extensive
 consultation, the Payments System Board concluded that a package of reforms to remove card surcharging,
 reduce interchange fee caps and improve transparency of payment costs would be in the public interest.
 Card surcharging was removed from 1 October and we have been monitoring the payments industry’s
 implementation and working with industry stakeholders to support merchant awareness of the changes. So
 far, several large providers have reduced their card processing fees for small businesses. We are also
 seeing signs of increased competition, with businesses shopping around and providers responding by
 offering more competitive pricing. These developments are welcome.
 Following amendments to the Payment Systems (Regulation) Act 1998 , which expanded our
 regulatory remit, we started a broader Review of Payments System Regulation with the publication of an
 Issues Paper in June. This Review is considering how regulation should respond to rapid innovation and
 change in the payments landscape, including opportunities to improve competition, efficiency and safety.
 In the submissions, stakeholders frequently raised issues relating to mobile wallets, three-party card
 schemes, account-to-account payments and agentic commerce. We recently published the stakeholder
 submissions and a summary of them. We intend to release regulatory priorities by the end of 2026 and
 start further consultation on prioritised issues by mid-2027.
 In May, we published the Project Acacia Final Report, which found that the tokenisation of assets and
 money, alongside upgrades to market infrastructure, has the potential to enhance the efficiency and
 resilience of Australia’s wholesale financial markets. Coordination challenges across the financial
 system have meant that these innovations have yet to scale. However, momentum around tokenised finance is
 now building in Australia along various lines – as it is internationally – and following the
 post-Acacia roadmap, we have continued to progress various initiatives to support responsible innovation.

RBA TRIMMED MEAN CPI, THE KEY CORE MEASURE, ROSE 1.0% QOQ, IN LINE WITH THE POLL, AND 3.7% YOY, ABOVE THE POLL OF 3.6%, WITH THE WEIGHTED MEDIAN CPI UP 1.0% QOQ AND 3.6% YOY
RBA Governor Bullock: Achieving price stability while maintaining full employment remains central to the RBA’s policy objectives.
RBA Governor Bullock: Although elevated borrowing costs are challenging for households and businesses, persistent inflation cannot be tolerated.
RBA Governor Bullock: The effects of monetary tightening take time to filter through the economy, meaning the impact of recent rate hikes has yet to fully materialise.
RBA Governor Bullock: Economic activity has experienced only a relatively limited impact from the ongoing conflict in the Middle East so far.
RBA Governor Bullock: Consumer spending continues to slow, but the pace of moderation remains gradual.
